opus-5.5.text:
I think foundation models have changed end-to-end AI in a quite fundamental way, and the shift is easy to underestimate.

For decades AI was built as a pipeline. In autonomous driving you had perception, then prediction, then planning, then control, each a separate module with its own team, data, and hand-written rules connecting them. Speech, translation, and search worked the same way. Every interface between modules was a place where information got lost and errors piled up. End-to-end learning was always the dream, going straight from raw input to the final decision, but in practice it rarely worked well. The models weren't big enough, we didn't have enough data, and the systems didn't generalize beyond what they had seen.

Foundation models changed that equation in three ways.

First, representation. A large model pre-trained on massive amounts of text, images, video, and now sensor data learns a very rich, general understanding of the world. You no longer have to engineer features for each subtask. The model has already absorbed much of the structure, so an end-to-end system starts from a strong prior rather than from scratch.

Second, generalization. The old modular systems were brittle. They handled the cases you designed for and failed at the long tail. Foundation models show emergent abilities: some reasoning, some common sense, the ability to handle situations they weren't explicitly trained on. For driving, robotics, or anything in the physical world, the long tail is the whole problem, so this matters enormously.

Third, the interface between humans and machines and between modules is now language, or more broadly tokens. Vision, language, and action can be put into one shared space. That's why we're seeing vision-language-action models, where a single model sees, understands, and acts. That is truly end-to-end, and it was very hard to imagine even five or six years ago.

I usually describe this as AI moving from information intelligence to physical intelligence and then to biological intelligence. Foundation models first transformed the information world: search, content, coding. Now the same end-to-end paradigm is moving into physical intelligence, meaning autonomous driving, robots, and drones. Beyond that it reaches biological intelligence, connecting with the human body, the brain, and life sciences.

I want to be honest about the challenges too. End-to-end systems are less interpretable. When a modular system fails, you can tell which module broke. When an end-to-end model fails, it's much harder to explain why. For safety-critical applications like driving or medicine, that's a real concern. So in practice I think we'll see a hybrid period for some time: an end-to-end foundation model at the core, with safety guardrails, verifiable rules, and redundancy around it. Data is also a bottleneck in the physical world. Internet text is plentiful, but high-quality real-world interaction data is scarce and expensive, so simulation, synthetic data, and world models will become very important.

But the direction is clear. Foundation models turned end-to-end from an academic ideal into an engineering reality. I believe this is one of the most important structural changes in AI in the past decade, perhaps bigger than any single model breakthrough, because it changes how we build intelligent systems in the first place.

r001.rationale: It says end-to-end learning rarely worked in practice before, then states foundation models turned it from an academic ideal into an engineering reality.

r002.rationale: It describes vision, language, and action in a shared token space, but does not identify a shared transformer architecture replacing input-specific algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Let me put it this way. Before foundation models, what we called end-to-end AI was really a modular pipeline. Take autonomous driving, which I spent several years on at Baidu. You had perception, then prediction, then planning, then control, each one its own module, each with its own engineers, its own rules, its own hand-tuned parameters. When a problem showed up, you went in and patched one module. That worked, but it hit a ceiling very quickly, because the real world has a long tail of situations no rule writer anticipated.

Foundation models changed two things fundamentally. The first is scale. We learned that if you give a model enough data and enough compute, it learns representations that generalize far beyond the specific cases it was shown. The second, and I think this is the deeper point, is that these models collapsed the boundaries between modules. In language, you no longer need separate systems for parsing, for translation, for summarization. One model does all of it. And that same lesson now applies to physical intelligence. In driving, we are seeing systems that go from camera input directly to trajectory, with the intermediate representations learned rather than designed.

So I understand the change as a shift in where human effort goes. In the old paradigm, the human was inside the system, designing every interface. In the new paradigm, the human defines the objective and the data, and the model learns the system itself. That is what "end-to-end" truly means now.

I would add one caveat. End-to-end does not mean black box with no structure. The best systems I have seen still have world models, still have memory, still have some way of reasoning about physics and causality. The architecture is learned, but the inductive biases still matter. And for safety-critical domains like driving or robotics, we still need interpretability and verification. So the foundation model gives us the capability, but turning that into a trustworthy product is still a lot of engineering. That is where I spend most of my attention now at Tsinghua, on how these models become embodied in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models enabled learned, direct camera-to-trajectory systems, but does not clearly state that end-to-end AI approaches were previously infeasible.

r002.rationale: It describes one model handling multiple language tasks and a similar lesson applying to driving, but does not identify a shared transformer architecture across different input types.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models have changed both what we mean by end-to-end and how we achieve it. In the past, we often divided an AI system into separate modules: perception, understanding, reasoning, and action. We optimized each module, but putting them together was difficult. An improvement in one component did not necessarily improve the whole system.

With foundation models, we can train across many tasks and types of data using a shared representation. That creates the possibility of a much more direct connection between an input and the desired output. Instead of building a new pipeline for every application, we start with a general model and adapt it.

But I would distinguish end-to-end learning from having a complete, reliable system. A model can produce a very convincing answer without being correct. And when you move from generating text to controlling a robot or driving a car, errors have physical consequences. You still need verification, constraints, and ways to handle uncertainty.

So the fundamental change is that we have a more general foundation for intelligence. The next challenge is connecting that intelligence to action—and making the entire process reliable, rather than simply making the model larger.

r001.rationale: It contrasts difficult, separately optimized modules with foundation models that make a direct input-to-output approach possible.

r002.rationale: It describes a shared representation and general model across tasks and data types, but does not identify a shared transformer architecture replacing input-specific algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models have fundamentally changed what we mean by end-to-end AI. In the past, we often built a system for a specific task: we collected labeled data, trained a model, and connected it to other components. Even when we called it end-to-end, the scope was usually quite narrow.

Now, a model can learn a broad set of capabilities through large-scale pretraining, and we can adapt those capabilities to many different tasks. Language becomes an interface for expressing intent, while multimodal models can connect language with images, audio, and other inputs. That reduces the amount of task-specific engineering we need.

But we should distinguish an end-to-end model from an end-to-end system. Producing a good answer is one thing; taking an action reliably in the real world is another. You still need feedback, verification, and ways to handle mistakes. So the major change is that we have a much more general foundation. The next challenge is to turn that foundation into systems that can perceive, reason, act, and learn from the results.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models broaden capabilities and reduce task-specific engineering, but does not state that they made previously infeasible end-to-end AI approaches feasible.

r002.rationale: It mentions multimodal models connecting language with images and audio, but does not identify a shift from input-specific algorithms to a shared transformer architecture.
